books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
The Rise of the Modern American City

primary_sources: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stimulus.text:
“Long ago it was said that “one half of the world does not know how the other half lives.” That was true then. It did not know because it did not care. The half that was on top cared little for the struggles, and less for the fate of those who were underneath, so long as it was able to hold them there and keep its own seat.”

“To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them. The fifteen thousand tenant houses that were the despair of the sanitarian in the past generation have swelled into thirty-seven thousand, and more than twelve hundred thousand persons call them home.”

(Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890, Introduction)
stimulus.source_note: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (Charles Scribner's Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain; wording checked against the Project Gutenberg text.

stem: Riis wrote for a middle-class audience that could vote, give money, and press for laws. His opening lines best show that his purpose was to

options.text: prove that tenement life was comfortable and healthy for families
options.misconception: Riis describes crowding and suffering, not comfort.

options.text: make comfortable readers feel responsible for conditions they had ignored
advertise tenement apartments to wealthy buyers
options.misconception: Riis exposes tenements; he does not advertise them.

options.text: defend tenement landlords against their critics
options.misconception: Riis was a reformer who exposed landlords; he did not defend them.

rationales.A: The passage calls the tenements crowded and the story dark. Comfort is the opposite of Riis's picture.
rationales.B: Riis tells the comfortable half that it did not know because it did not care, and that the half underneath suffered. The charge is meant to move readers to act.
rationales.C: No advertisement is in the passage. Riis writes to expose, not to sell.
rationales.D: Riis blames the community that gave the poor no other choice. Landlords are part of that blame, not its defense.
rationales.general:
Ask whom the passage addresses and what it asks of them.
1. The passage speaks to the half on top, the comfortable readers.
2. It charges them: they did not know because they did not care.
3. It then shows the crowding those readers had ignored.
4. The charge plus the evidence is a call to take responsibility and support reform.
Remember: a passage that accuses its reader is asking the reader to act.
